newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE - China advertisers find sky is the limit.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - China advertisers find sky is the limit.

text.p: Some joint ventures in China never get off the ground but that hasn't been the case with one Singapore company that has set up China's first commercial blimp operation.
With an eye to the rapid rise in advertising spending in this nation of 1.2 billion people, Singapore's Thakral Group has found a way to give its corporate profile a lift.

The blimp -- seen hovering over the nation's capital with its message of which brand of beer to swill or mobile phone to dial -- has been described as an unidentified flying object by some imaginative Chinese copy writers.
Less imagination is needed at night when the 39-metre helium airship -- about the length of a 737 jet -- flies illuminated in the sky.
"We thought this was a way to do something different for the marketplace," said Francis Chiew, general manager of Beijing Orient Air Service Company Ltd.
While blimps have long been used in advertising in the West, China has only recently allowed its first commercial lighter-than-air ship to go aloft.

Thakral, engaged in trading and the distribution of electronics goods, formed its joint venture in 1994 and had its first flight the following year. But the business got its real vote of confidence only recently with its first long-term contract from Finnish mobile phone supplier Nokia AB Oy.
China is estimated to have spent some $1.1 billion on advertising last year, up 34 percent from the previous year.
Its nearly 10 percent economic growth and rising living standards are a magnet for foreign firms, eager to sell their goods.
"As more and more multi-nationals come to China to get a piece of the China market, there is a need for a marketing medium," said Chiew.
"Airship advertising, we believe, would be a way to do that," he said.
BUSINESS BARRIERS
Chiew and other officials at Beijing Orient concede that China has placed a few obstructions across their flight path.
"We had to deal with a lot of bureaucracy to explain the concept," said Chiew.
Selling the idea to customers was also an uphill battle.
"This has been proven in Europe and the United States but not here. We had no statistics," Chiew said, adding that the company had a difficult first year.

One other hurdle is that the military controls the nation's airspace. So Thakral turned to a partner with the right connections, and it found Beilei Science and Technology Development, which owns 25 percent of the $3 million venture.
While officials are reticent about the Chinese partner's background, many of the employees are former air force personnel.
On the ground, members of the People's Armed Police, or paramilitary forces, help with the airship's takeoffs and landings in a rice field on the outskirts of Beijing.
There are other rules to observe in this business in Beijing. The blimp cannot fly above the city centre where most people live and work -- and the Communist Party has it headquarters.
NO MUSIC, PLEASE
It also is not supposed to play music or make announcements, company officials tell reporters, nearly shouting over the din of a loudspeaker from an army base near the blimp's Beijing home.
Some of the problems are less artificial.
"I remember the first flight -- there were really high winds," said Li Lei, one of the ground maintenance men who keep the U.S.-built, propeller-driven ship airworthy.
Beijing Orient notes that not every company wanting to make an impact on China's consumers will be ready to take its message to the air. Renting the blimp can cost $12,000 a day.
But that compares with a 30-second, prime time advertisement on state televison costing at least 50,000 yuan ($6,000), making Beijing Orient believe it still has a competitive product.
And how much business is out there? The sky's the limit.
